title: What it takes to operate a SaaS when AI agents write all the code
content:
AI agents can now do a lot of the work I used to do to build DocSpring. That's exciting when I look at my backlog, and slightly less comfortable when I think about someone else using the same tools to build a competing product.
Nico Jeannen wrote about this on X: AI has made basic SaaS products much easier to build and copy. He was responding to Olly's post about founder exhaustion and the worry that AI could make their businesses redundant. I understand both reactions.
DocSpring fills and generates PDFs and Word documents, and collects e-signatures. I founded it as FormAPI, and our team now uses AI agents throughout development and operations. I spend far less time writing code myself. I've also been working harder than ever.
I'm finally working through feature ideas and bugs that sat in the backlog for years. But even with agents doing much of the implementation, running the business takes a lot of attention. Customers keep using what we've already shipped while we decide what to change next. Each change has to fit the product they're relying on.
Building the document platform I had in mind
Agents are saving me so much time that it keeps changing what I think we can build.
One of the main reasons I renamed FormAPI to DocSpring was that I wanted to build a broader document automation platform. Filling PDF forms was the starting point. I wanted people to be able to create and automate other kinds of documents too, but there was always more work to do on the product we already had.
We've now shipped Word templates and the Page Designer. You can upload a Word document with placeholders and fill it with data, or design a document directly in the browser without starting from an existing file. These are two features I wasn't sure I'd ever get around to building. Seeing them in the product makes the name DocSpring feel much closer to what I had in mind when I chose it.
Our release notes show how much else has changed over the last few months. Alongside those new template types, we've redesigned the website and the app, and shipped API v2. E-signing has had a huge amount of work too, including signer roles and emails to send signing links, reminders, and completed documents.
One e-signing problem had been stuck for a particularly long time: figuring out how to seal PDFs with a certificate trusted through the Adobe Approved Trust List. We've finally settled the approach, although we're still waiting for the certificate to be issued. That work involved researching certificate providers and their requirements as well as writing the sealing code. Having an agent help with that research let us make progress on something I had struggled to figure out for years. When I researched this myself a few years ago, it was prohibitively expensive for a small startup, with contracts starting at $50k per year. AI agents helped me research and reach out to every vendor we could find, and we've finally found a vendor who can supply a certificate for only a few thousand dollars per year. We can also bring our own cloud HSM. (Other vendors will only send you a certificate on a USB stick that you have to plug into a physical server.)
We've also reached things further down the backlog. Side-by-side previews now work across every template type, so you can keep the filled document visible while editing. A customer had asked for this years ago, and it kept getting pushed further down our backlog as new, more urgent tickets kept piling up. I simply wasn't able to get around to it when I had to write all the code and fix all the bugs myself. We also rebuilt our Alpaca.js web forms with react-jsonschema-form, which generates React forms from a JSON schema, and added form sections so a long form can be split into steps.
These are projects I would once have had to tackle one after another, and each one would have taken me weeks or months. Now an AI session can work on how a Word document renders while another works on how a long form is split into sections. I move between them when they need a decision, while implementation and review continue in the other sessions.
Keeping all of this moving
This period in time reminds me of the first few months of building FormAPI, when I worked on it non-stop. Work, eat, sleep, repeat. Now a difficult dependency or infrastructure problem doesn't necessarily mean putting all the product work aside. An agent can investigate it and bring me a reproduction or a proposed fix while I work with another session. I currently use Herdr to manage 49 different Claude Code sessions that each focus on a different task or product area. 26 of these sessions are currently "active", and only a dozen or so will be working on things in parallel. I often have a long list of sessions that are waiting for me to read something and make a decision, so I spend my days jumping between sessions, mostly reading updates and answering questions. The rapid context switching was difficult at the beginning, and I would end each day utterly exhausted. But I've been getting used to this workflow, and I don't find it so challenging anymore.
Some of those Claude Code sessions have an ongoing job. I have one that works through big batches of bug fixes, taking a collection of smaller problems through investigation, implementation, and review. Another is devoted to Sentry, the service that reports errors from our application. It investigates the errors, works on fixes, and sorts out which reports are noise that we can ignore. The bug backlog and the errors showing up in the running product both get attention while other agents work on new features.
I have a separate session for performance. Its job is to investigate slow pages and make sure the app feels fast to use. Recent work has involved tracing slow database queries, changing indexes and how we fetch records, and measuring the result after deployment. Another agent works on our CI pipeline (the automated checks that run when we push code). With so many branches being worked on, I care about both how quickly those checks finish and what they cost. We've moved many jobs onto my home servers, while keeping the option to run them in CircleCI's cloud. The agent works on the pipeline itself so the other sessions can keep getting their changes tested.
These jobs used to compete much more directly with feature work for my time. Now I can have agents working on reliability and performance while other sessions build the bigger things I want to launch. I still have to set priorities and review what they propose, but choosing to work on a new feature doesn't mean all of that maintenance has to wait. Product changes still go through automated checks, code review, and staging QA before production. Having more work in progress makes that process more important, and agents do much of the work of running checks, reviewing changes, and fixing what they find.
Our Sorbet work would have been hard for me to justify before I started working with AI agents. Sorbet is a type checker for Ruby. Agents helped us type the application, and then we built our own plugins so it could understand more of our Rails code and templates. Maintaining a customized type checker is the sort of project I once assumed was out of reach alongside everything else we needed to do.
Finishing these projects still involves our team reviewing the result and getting it released. We've built Rack Gateway so agents can prepare server commands and deployments and bring me the actual code or commit to approve. That saves me from assembling each operation myself. It also puts the proposed change in front of me while I can still stop it.
The work also arrives faster now. Several sessions can make progress independently and then need a decision at once. A patch can be ready for review while a customer conversation raises a new question about the same feature. I have to bring that customer context back to the implementation before we ship it. report.summary: DocSpring's founder explains how AI agents now write most of his code, letting him ship long-stalled features — yet review, operations and constant context-switching still consume his days.
report.background: Coding agents have moved in the past year from autocomplete to autonomous, multi-file work that can run for hours without supervision. That shift has triggered a debate among SaaS founders: if agents can rebuild a basic product quickly, what protects an existing business? Nico Jeannen argued on X that AI makes simple SaaS products easier to build and copy, replying to another founder's post about exhaustion and the fear of becoming redundant. DocSpring, founded as FormAPI, is a small document-automation company that fills PDFs and Word files and collects e-signatures — exactly the kind of focused product the debate is about. Its founder's answer is not to retreat but to point agents at years of backlog, while discovering that orchestration, prioritisation and human judgement become the new bottleneck rather than implementation.
key_points: Agents cleared a backlog that had been stuck for years. DocSpring shipped Word templates, a browser Page Designer, a website and app redesign, API v2, signer roles and e-signature emails — projects the founder says would each have taken weeks or months when he wrote every line himself.

AI research broke a long-standing dead end. Sealing PDFs with a certificate trusted by the Adobe Approved Trust List once meant contracts starting at $50k a year; agents helped research and contact every vendor, landing a certificate for a few thousand a year, with bring-your-own cloud HSM supported.

The founder now orchestrates 49 Claude Code sessions through a tool called Herdr, with roughly a dozen working in parallel. His days are spent jumping between sessions, reading updates and answering questions — context switching he initially found exhausting.

Some agents hold permanent jobs: one grinds through batches of bug fixes, one triages Sentry error reports and filters noise, one investigates slow queries and indexes, and one maintains the CI pipeline for speed and cost, moving jobs onto home servers.

Nothing ships without guardrails. Changes still pass automated checks, code review and staging QA, and a tool called Rack Gateway lets agents prepare server commands and deployments that the founder must explicitly approve before they run.
report.impact: The piece reframes the AI-and-SaaS debate: the moat is not the code but customer trust, operational discipline and taste in prioritisation. For developers, it shows a credible working model — many parallel agent sessions, always-on maintenance agents, and strict review gates — and it shows the cost, which is relentless decision-making rather than typing. For the industry, it suggests small teams can now sustain products that previously needed headcount, narrowing the gap between solo founders and funded competitors, while raising new questions about review capacity, CI costs and audit trails. For regular users, the near-term effect is faster shipping of long-requested features, alongside the risk that products built cheaply are also copied cheaply.
report.tools: Worth watching: Claude Code (the agent runtime used here), Herdr (orchestrates dozens of parallel sessions), Rack Gateway (agent-prepared deploys with human approval), Sentry (error monitoring and triage), Sorbet with custom Rails plugins (Ruby type checking), react-jsonschema-form (JSON-schema-driven forms), and CircleCI for CI. For readers building similar workflows, start with one always-on maintenance agent plus strict review gates before scaling to many parallel sessions.
